podcast.title: First Wave Decline (December 1956)
podcast.body: By December 1956, the initial surge of rockabilly music was largely over, with many prominent artists like Carl Perkins, Gene Vincent, and Bill Haley no longer having chart successes. Only Elvis Presley remained a leading white rock and roll star from this era. "We're coming to the end of 1956, and with it, the end of the first wave of rockabilly."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 51: "Matchbox" by Carl Perkins

podcast.title: Transition to Country Music (Post-1956)
podcast.body: After December 4, 1956, artists like Carl Perkins and Johnny Cash increasingly moved away from rockabilly and towards country music. This date is seen as a border between periods in rock and roll history, before rock and roll became the dominant genre. "They both moved increasingly towards country music, and away from rockabilly."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 51: "Matchbox" by Carl Perkins

podcast.title: Homage in The Cramps' Work (1986)
podcast.body: The Cramps' 1986 album, *A Date with Elvis*, was explicitly conceived as an homage to rockabilly music, showcasing their deep roots in the genre. "Adate with Elvis, un homenaje al Riddel Rock."

srcs.source: Central Sonora
srcs.episode: Amor, Terror y Psychobilly: La Historia de The Cramps

podcast.title: Influence on George Michael's "Faith" (1987)
podcast.body: George Michael's song "Faith" featured a retro sound that was an explicit homage to Rockabilly. "This homage to Rockabilly came with an iconic music video."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
srcs.episode: Hits of the Year Edition Part 2

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
srcs.episode: Hits of the Year Edition Part 2

podcast.title: "Go Go Go" as a Classic
podcast.body: Roy Orbison's co-written B-side "Go Go Go" to "Ooby Dooby" was recorded in a single take and became a significant rockabilly classic. It was later covered by Jerry Lee Lewis and remained one of the few rockabilly songs Orbison kept in his set lists throughout his career. "The B side was recorded in a single take and itself became a rockabilly classic."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 42: "Ooby Dooby" by Roy Orbison and the Teen Kings

podcast.title: "Hillbilly Bop" Label for Elvis
podcast.body: In the early years of his career, Elvis Presley's music was sometimes referred to by interviewers as "Hillbilly Bop." This term highlighted the fusion of country music and the colloquial understanding of "Bbapp" (bop) that characterized early rockabilly. "You would often find interviewers talking with Elvis in his early years, referring to his music as Hillbilly Bop, or a mixture of country music and Bbapp."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 41: "Be-Bop-A-Lula" by Gene Vincent and the Bluecaps

podcast.title: Amateur Enthusiasm Welcome
podcast.body: Rockabilly, as a genre, was notable for its acceptance of "enthusiastic amateurs" more than most other musical styles. This characteristic contributed to its raw and unpolished sound, which was often embraced by its audience. "rockabilly, more than most genres, was comfortable with enthusiastic amateurs anyway."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 41: "Be-Bop-A-Lula" by Gene Vincent and the Bluecaps

podcast.title: Aversion to Mainstream, Affinity for Obscure (Mid-1970s)
podcast.body: In the mid-1970s, Poison Ivy and Lux Interior developed a strong dislike for the progressive rock and singer-songwriter music dominating record stores. They instead became avid collectors of rockabilly, especially its more obscure B-sides, along with doo-wop and 60s garage rarities from second-hand bins. "El duro Waps se convirtió en su feticche, pero también las rarezas de garage de los años 60 y sobretodo el rockabilly. Se volvieron unos enfermos coleccionistas de esa música, en especial de las caras v más oscuras."

srcs.source: Central Sonora
srcs.episode: Amor, Terror y Psychobilly: La Historia de The Cramps

podcast.title: Backstage Jam Sessions for Development
podcast.body: The backstage area of the Saturday Night Jamboree at the Goodwin Institute Auditorium was a critical environment for the development of many early rockabilly acts, where musicians would informally jam, share new riffs, and exchange musical ideas. "Those backstage jam sessions were the making of the Ruck and Roll trio as they were for many of the other Ruckabilly acts in the area."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 44: "Train Kept A-Rollin'", by Johnny Burnette and the Rock 'n' Roll Trio

podcast.title: Birth in Sun Studios
podcast.body: The distinctive rockabilly sound was "in essence, created in Sun Studios." This genre truly began to define itself after Elvis Presley's departure from Sun Records, when Sam Phillips intensified his efforts to produce records that encapsulated this specific style, moving beyond it being solely identified with a single artist. "The rockabilly sound was, in essence, created in Sun Studios"

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 36: "Blue Suede Shoes" by Carl Perkins

podcast.title: Charlie Gillett's Typology
podcast.body: Identified by Charlie Gillett as synonymous with Memphis Country Rock, one of the five distinct styles he identified within early rock and roll. "Memphis Country Rock, the music we normally talk about as rockabilly."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 8: The Fat Man and Fats Domino

podcast.title: Defining a Subgenre
podcast.body: The true rockabilly era saw its major figures emerge from Sun Studios, establishing a sound often used as a benchmark. While country-influenced white rock and rollers like Buddy Holly and the Everly Brothers appeared in 1957 and were sometimes called rockabilly, aficionados often excluded them if their sound deviated significantly from the Sun Studios style. "We're pretty much at the end of the true rockabilly era already."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 63: "Susie Q", by Dale Hawkins

podcast.title: Disappearance from Charts (Late 1950s)
podcast.body: By the time Elvis Presley returned from the army in 1960, rockabilly music had "totally disappeared from their charts." This shift prompted many musicians who had emerged with Elvis to pivot to other genres like orchestrated pop or country. "Rockabilly had totally disappeared from their charts."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 82: "Are You Lonesome Tonight?" by Elvis Presley

podcast.title: Early Irwin Records Releases
podcast.body: Irwin Records, owned by Irwin Ellis, released a handful of rockabilly classics, including Hoi Jackson's "In-Gloves" and Ray Scott's "Bop in Week 1 Willie." "he did manage to release a handful of rockabilly classics on Irwin Records, like Hoj Jackson's in- gloves. And Bop in Week 1 Willie by Ray Scott"

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 105: "Green Onions" by Booker T.and the MGs

podcast.title: Extreme Expression of Early Rock and Roll
podcast.body: Rockabilly singers, like Billy Lee Riley, pushed the nascent rock and roll genre to its extremes in the 1950s, with performances that were even more radical than the already subversive acts of the time. "Billy Lee was taking this music to extremes."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt-Rock: Chapter 1

podcast.title: Female Performers and Genre Mixing
podcast.body: It was common for female performers, particularly those transitioning into rock and roll from other genres, to mix styles within a single song. This often involved having a verse in one style and a chorus in another (as Wanda Jackson did with "I Gotta Know") or other combinations (like Kay Starr's "Rock and Roll Waltz"). This ambiguity allowed established stars to hedge their bets, portraying the music as either a parody or a mockery of new styles, in case rock and roll proved to be a temporary fad.

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 43: "I Gotta Know" by Wanda Jackson

podcast.title: Funding by Elvis-RCA Deal
podcast.body: The entire genre of rockabilly was effectively funded by the cash that Sun Records received from the unprecedented deal that signed Elvis Presley over to RCA Records. "It's safe to say that the whole genre of rockabilly was funded by that one deal."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 38: "Heartbreak Hotel" by Elvis Presley

podcast.title: George Michael's Genre Versatility
podcast.body: George Michael's multi-platinum album "Faith" demonstrated his imperial versatility, generating hits like the rockabilly title track alongside funk pop and soul ballads. "ranging from the funk pop of I Want Your Sex to the Rockabilly title track to the Soul Ballad's father figure and one more try."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
srcs.episode: Material Girl in an Imperial World Edition Part 1

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
srcs.episode: Material Girl in an Imperial World Edition Part 1

podcast.title: Gretsch Popularity
podcast.body: Following its success with country players, Gretsch guitars found popularity among rockabilly artists, which then led to their adoption by early rock and rollers. "From there, it's used spread to rockabilly artists and finally to the new rock and rollers at the late 1950s."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Story of the Electric Guitar - Part 2

podcast.title: Hero of the Genre – Mojo Nixon
podcast.body: Mojo Nixon is recognized as a "Rockabilly, punkabilly hero," highlighting his significant status within these genres. "What are my favorite writers belong to the late Rockabilly, punkabilly hero, Mojo Nixon?"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Backstage Rider

podcast.title: Influence on Elvis Costello
podcast.body: Elvis Costello's 1981 album "Trust" demonstrated his expanding musical interests, with songs alluding to various styles, including rockabilly. This indicated his willingness to incorporate diverse influences into his new wave sound. "with songs alluding to jazz, rockabilly, even country."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
srcs.episode: Angry Young Men Edition Part 2

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
srcs.episode: Angry Young Men Edition Part 2

podcast.title: Ken Nelson's Misunderstanding
podcast.body: Ken Nelson, the head of country music at Capitol Records, despite his expertise in country, "didn't really understand rock-a-billy at all." This lack of comprehension influenced his decisions, such as suggesting unsuitable material for rockabilly artists like Gene Vincent. "Nelson didn't really understand rock-a-billy at all..."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 41: "Be-Bop-A-Lula" by Gene Vincent and the Bluecaps

podcast.title: Memphis Rockabilly from Satellite
podcast.body: Satellite Records also tried its hand at rockabilly, notably with Don Willis's "But in High School Baby," described as a "prime slice of Memphis rockabilly" known for its heavy slapback echo. "But in high school baby by Dunn Willis is a prime slice of Memphis rockabilly, though one with so much slapback echo that even Joe Meek might have said, Hangong isn't that a bit much."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 105: "Green Onions" by Booker T.and the MGs

podcast.title: Nick Lowe's Return to Pop Chart
podcast.body: Nick Lowe returned to the pop chart in the mid-1980s with the rockabilly-flavored song "Half a Boy and Half a Man." This track, accompanied by a retro beachy video, showcased the genre's enduring appeal and Lowe's ability to infuse classic styles with contemporary relevance. "Nick Lo returned to the pop chart with the Rockabilly flavored Half a Boy and Half a Man."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
srcs.episode: Angry Young Men Edition Part 2

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
srcs.episode: Angry Young Men Edition Part 2

podcast.title: Origins in California Western Swing
podcast.body: Rockabilly music originated from the western swing created by Dust Bowl migrants in California during the 1940s. This music, influenced by blues and boogie woogie, then made its way eastward to Tennessee, where it "transmuted itself into rockability." Jack Guthrie's "Oki Boogie" is cited as a clear precursor.

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 43: "I Gotta Know" by Wanda Jackson

podcast.title: Past Trend
podcast.body: Rockabilly is mentioned as a past musical trend, questioning if anyone is "still into rock ability." "Anyone still into rock ability?"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Good Goth: Part 2

podcast.title: Purist Definition
podcast.body: For purists, rockabilly holds a "very, very specific meaning" regarding its sonic characteristics. It mandates the presence of slapback echo on vocals, an electric guitar, and slapback bass, essentially mirroring the core elements of Elvis Presley's earliest recordings. While piano or drums could be added (to accommodate artists like Jerry Lee Lewis), the sound strictly prohibits horns, strings, or backing vocals to maintain its primitive quality. Furthermore, steel guitar or fiddle are excluded to prevent it from crossing over into country music territory. "It had to have slapback echo on the vocals. It had to have an electrically guitar and slapback bass."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 36: "Blue Suede Shoes" by Carl Perkins

podcast.title: Slapback Bass as a Defining Feature
podcast.body: Slapback double bass is considered one of the defining features of the rockabilly genre. This characteristic distinguished it from later innovations like the electric bass, which was a deliberate choice by Dale Hawkins to move towards an electric blues sound. "slapback bass is one of the defining features of the rockabilly genre."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 63: "Susie Q", by Dale Hawkins

podcast.title: Successor to Ska in Press Favor
podcast.body: Rockabilly was declared the "next big thing" by an editor or writer in the British music press, leading to an overnight abandonment of Ska by the media. "some editor or writer decided that rockabilly was the next big thing and everyone abandoned SCA almost overnight."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt-Rock: Chapter 9

podcast.title: Sun Records' Heyday
podcast.body: Rockabilly experienced a four-year heyday at Sun Records, during which Sam Phillips and Jack Clement recorded thousands of songs by numerous artists. These recordings became a crucial part of Sun's extensive back catalog, later systematically reissued by labels like Charlie. "In their four-year Rocket Billy Hayday, Sam Phillips and Jack Clements had recorded literally thousands of unreleased songs by Jerry Lee Lewis, Johnny Cash, Roy Orbison, Karl Perkins, Conway Twitty, Charlie Rich, Billy Lee Riley, and more."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 66: "Great Balls of Fire" by Jerry Lee Lewis
